title: HE HAD 14 WIVES, 22 SONS, AND 16 DAUGHTERS… BUT THE MOST SHOCKING THING ABOUT THIS KING WASN’T HIS FAMILY.
paragraphs: HE HAD 14 WIVES, 22 SONS, AND 16 DAUGHTERS… BUT THE MOST SHOCKING THING ABOUT THIS KING WASN’T HIS FAMILY.

Buried in one of the Bible’s most overlooked passages is the story of a king surrounded by wealth, power, and fifty-two children. Yet behind the royal household lies a devastating question about the difference between possessing everything this world admires and having a heart that truly belongs to God.
“And Abijah waxed mighty, and married fourteen wives, and begat twenty and two sons, and sixteen daughters.” — 2 Chronicles 13:21 (KJV)
Fifty-two children.
Fourteen wives.
One king.
And a spiritual warning that reaches far beyond the walls of ancient Jerusalem.

Imagine walking through a royal palace where children are running through courtyards, servants are preparing meals, and the voices of an enormous family echo through corridors decorated with the treasures of a kingdom.

Imagine the celebrations when another son is born. The excitement when another daughter enters the household. The elaborate ceremonies, the political alliances, the royal garments, the endless responsibilities of maintaining a family larger than most villages could imagine.
Now imagine standing in the middle of all that abundance...
And discovering that none of it can tell you whether the man sitting on the throne truly loves God.
Because that is where the story of King Abijah becomes uncomfortable.
Not because the Bible tells us he had fourteen wives.
Not even because it tells us he fathered fifty-two children.
But because another passage reveals something about his heart that his impressive household could never conceal.
And if we are willing to listen, his story may expose something about our own.
Something we have been hiding behind our achievements, our religious activity, our public reputation, or even our blessings.
Stay with this story.
Because the greatest tragedy is not always losing everything.
Sometimes it is having almost everything people dream about while remaining spiritually divided within.
Abijah was not an ordinary man.
He was a descendant of King David, the son of Rehoboam, and the ruler of Judah during a dangerous period in Israel's history.

The kingdom had already been torn apart following the reign of Solomon. Ten northern tribes had separated from the Davidic dynasty, while Judah and Benjamin remained under the southern kingdom centered in Jerusalem.
The wounds of national division were still fresh.
The people who had once belonged to one united kingdom were now facing one another across battle lines.
And Abijah inherited a throne surrounded by conflict.
According to 2 Chronicles 13:1–2, he began reigning during the eighteenth year of Jeroboam's rule over Israel.
His reign lasted three years.
Only three.
Think about that.
Fourteen wives. Fifty-two children. A royal dynasty. A military campaign recorded in Scripture.
And only three years on the throne.

The Bible does not tell us precisely when he married each wife or when every child was born. We should not assume that all fifty-two children were born during those three years. His household may have been established over a much longer period of his life.
But Scripture does tell us something astonishing about the king's public declaration of faith.
When Abijah confronted Jeroboam and the northern army, he delivered a speech that sounded remarkably courageous.
He reminded Israel of God's covenant with David.
He defended the priesthood and worship established in Judah.
He challenged the northern kingdom's reliance on golden calves and unauthorized religious practices.
And then he declared:
“But as for us, the LORD is our God, and we have not forsaken him.” — 2 Chronicles 13:10 (KJV)
Those are powerful words.
The kind of words that could make an entire army stand taller.
The kind of words that sound like they belong on the lips of a faithful king.
And in the battle that followed, Judah cried out to the Lord, the priests sounded their trumpets, and God gave Judah victory over Jeroboam's forces.
Second Chronicles 13:18 explains why:
“Because they relied upon the LORD God of their fathers.” (KJV)
Read that carefully.
God truly helped Judah.
The victory was real.
The appeal to God's covenant was not meaningless.
And yet...
There is another passage.
A passage that changes how we understand the man behind the speech.
First Kings 15:3 says of Abijah, whose name is rendered Abijam in that account:
“And he walked in all the sins of his father, which he had done before him: and his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God, as the heart of David his father.” (KJV)
There it is.
The uncomfortable truth.
A king who could speak convincingly about God's covenant did not possess a heart wholly devoted to the God whose covenant he defended.
He could publicly defend true worship while personally following sinful patterns.
He could recognize the errors of another kingdom while failing to confront the divided loyalties within himself.
He could lead people in a moment of dependence upon God without consistently walking in wholehearted obedience.
And suddenly, Abijah's story is no longer just about an ancient king.
It is about the terrifying possibility of knowing how to speak about God without fully surrendering to Him.
How many of us know the right words?
We know when to say, “God is good.”
We know how to encourage someone with a Bible verse.
We know how to pray when a crisis arrives.
We know how to defend our beliefs when someone challenges Christianity.
But what happens when the crowd disappears?
When the church service ends?
When the phone is turned off?
When there is nobody left to impress?
What does God find in the private chambers of our hearts?
The Hebrew wording of 1 Kings 15:3 is especially revealing.
The passage describes Abijah's heart with the expression לֹא־הָיָה לְבָבוֹ שָׁלֵם (lo-hayah levavo shalem).
In context, it means that his heart was not wholly devoted to the LORD.
The Hebrew word shalem (שָׁלֵם) carries the sense of completeness or wholeness.
The issue was not that Abijah had failed to achieve flawless human perfection.
David himself committed grievous sins, including adultery and arranging the death of Uriah.
Yet David is used as the comparison because, despite his terrible failures, his life was characterized by a fundamental allegiance to the Lord, and Scripture records his repentance when confronted.
Abijah's heart, by contrast, was not described as wholly committed to God.
This distinction matters.
Because God is not looking for people who have never fallen.
If that were the requirement, none of us could stand before Him.
He calls sinners to repentance, faith, and wholehearted devotion.
And there is an enormous difference between struggling against sin and making peace with it.
Between falling and refusing to get up.
Between confessing our disobedience and constructing religious excuses to protect it.
Maybe you understand that difference more personally than you would like to admit.
Maybe there is something in your life that you keep defending even though you know God's Word is confronting it.
A relationship you refuse to surrender.
A habit you keep hiding.
A resentment you have nurtured for years.
A secret compromise that nobody in your church knows about.
Perhaps people admire your faith, but privately you know how exhausted you are from maintaining the appearance of spiritual strength.
You smile when people ask how you are doing.
You say, “I'm blessed.”
And perhaps you truly are grateful for God's blessings.
But somewhere beneath the smile, you are carrying a battle that nobody sees.
Abijah's story forces us to consider something we would rather avoid.
Public religious confidence is not the same thing as private spiritual faithfulness.
And God's willingness to show mercy in one area of our lives does not mean He approves of everything we are doing.
That is why the difference between the accounts in Chronicles and Kings is so important.
Chronicles emphasizes Abijah's confrontation with Jeroboam, his appeal to God's covenant, Judah's reliance on the Lord, and the victory God granted.
Kings evaluates the overall direction of Abijah's reign and his failure to remain wholly faithful.
These accounts are not necessarily contradictory.
They are showing different dimensions of the same king.
One reveals what happened when Judah relied on God.
The other reveals the spiritual condition of the ruler who stood before them.
And both truths must be allowed to speak.
God can act faithfully toward His covenant even when the human beings involved are deeply imperfect.
His mercy is not an endorsement of every action taken by those who receive it.
His faithfulness does not depend on the moral perfection of earthly rulers.
That should humble us.
Because some of us have mistaken surviving a crisis for receiving divine approval.
We prayed, and the door opened.
We cried, and help arrived.
We were in trouble, and somehow we escaped.
And instead of allowing God's kindness to lead us toward repentance, we quietly concluded that everything in our lives must be acceptable to Him.
But Romans 2:4 teaches that God's goodness is intended to lead us to repentance.
Mercy is an invitation.
Not permission to continue in rebellion.
And now we must return to those fourteen wives.
Because there is another detail we cannot afford to misunderstand.
Second Chronicles 13:21 records Abijah's marriages and children, but the verse does not explicitly declare that God approved of his polygamy.
It is a historical description, not a command for believers to imitate.
The Hebrew text includes the words וַיִּשָּׂא־לוֹ נָשִׁים אַרְבַּע עֶשְׂרֵה (vayyissa-lo nashim arba esreh), describing how he took fourteen wives.
The same verse reports twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters.
The numbers are straightforward.
But the moral interpretation requires the rest of Scripture.
Long before Abijah was born, Deuteronomy 17:17 warned concerning Israel's king:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away.” (KJV)
That warning was not accidental.
God understood the spiritual danger that could accompany royal excess, competing loyalties, and the pursuit of power through accumulated marriages.
Solomon's life had already demonstrated the danger.
First Kings 11 records that his many wives turned his heart toward other gods.
Scripture does not tell us that Abijah's fourteen wives caused his particular sins, and it would be irresponsible to invent private events within his household.
We are not told how he treated each wife.
We are not told what each child experienced.
We are not told whether his daughters felt loved or neglected.
We are not told whether his sons admired him or feared him.
Their individual stories are largely hidden from us.
And that silence deserves respect.
But we are told enough to recognize the broader warning.
A king could possess an extraordinary household while lacking wholehearted devotion to God.
And the same danger can appear in a completely different form today.
You may never sit on a throne.
You may never possess a palace.
You may never have fourteen spouses or fifty-two children.
But you can still spend your life multiplying things that cannot heal your soul.
More money.
More recognition.
More followers.
More accomplishments.
More possessions.
More approval.
More reasons for people to think you are successful.
Until one day you look around at everything you have built...
And realize you have neglected the One for whom you were created.
Jesus asked a question that cuts through every generation:
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” — Mark 8:36 (KJV)
That question does not lose its power when spoken to a king.
In fact, it becomes even more haunting.
Because a crown can conceal spiritual poverty.
A palace can contain profound loneliness.
And a person can be surrounded by people while remaining distant from God.
Perhaps the saddest part of Abijah's story is how quickly his earthly glory passed.
Three years.
That was his reign.
His strength, his royal household, and his military success did not make him immortal.
Eventually, another king occupied the throne.
Another generation inherited the consequences of the one before it.
Another name entered the royal records.
And Abijah became part of history.
Yet the Bible preserved something far more important than the dimensions of his palace or the splendor of his possessions.
It preserved the verdict concerning his heart.
Not wholly devoted.
Imagine that.
After all the things people could have remembered about you...
After every achievement, every promotion, every public victory, every expensive possession...
What if the most important truth about your life was something nobody could see except God?
That is a frightening thought.
But it can also become the beginning of freedom.
Because the Gospel does not leave us standing helpless beneath the weight of our failures.
It introduces us to a different King.
A King who did not come to multiply wives, accumulate political power, or preserve an earthly dynasty through royal ambition.
A King who came to save sinners.
His name is Jesus Christ.
And this is where the story moves from the tragedy of divided human hearts to the astonishing grace of God.
Abijah belonged to the royal line of David.
And the promise God made concerning David's house ultimately finds its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the Son of David.
Matthew 1:7 includes Abijah in the genealogy leading to Jesus.
Let that sink in.
Abijah.
The king whose heart was not wholly devoted to God.
The ruler whose life contained both a remarkable military victory and serious spiritual failure.
His name appears in the recorded ancestry of the Messiah.
Not because his sins were good.
Not because God approved of his disobedience.
Not because being part of a sacred family line automatically made him righteous.
But because God's redemptive purpose was greater than the failures of the people through whom the promised royal line continued.
And this is one of the most breathtaking truths in Scripture.
God's plan of salvation did not depend upon a spotless collection of human ancestors.
The genealogy of Jesus contains stories marked by scandal, sorrow, brokenness, judgment, mercy, and unexpected grace.
Yet the promised Savior came.
Not to excuse sin.
Not to celebrate rebellion.
But to defeat sin and redeem those who turn to Him.
Where earthly kings failed, Christ remained faithful.
Where human rulers pursued power, Jesus humbled Himself.
Where sinful hearts divided their loyalties, Jesus obeyed the Father perfectly.
And where we deserved judgment, Christ willingly bore the penalty of sin upon the cross.
Philippians 2:8 tells us:
“He humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.” (KJV)
Think of the contrast.
Abijah wore a crown and ruled for three years.
Jesus wore a crown of thorns, was crucified, and rose again.
Abijah's kingdom belonged to a divided nation.
Jesus proclaimed a kingdom that will never end.
Abijah's heart was not wholly devoted.
Jesus lived in perfect obedience.
And because of His death and resurrection, forgiveness and new life are offered to sinners who could never rescue themselves.
This is why the Gospel is not merely a message about becoming a better person.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ has accomplished what we could not accomplish.
He lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He died for sins He did not commit.
He rose from the dead.
And He calls us to repent and believe in Him.
The Greek of Mark 1:15 preserves that call:
μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ
Metanoeite kai pisteuete en tō euangeliō.
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” (KJV)
The word metanoeite calls for repentance—a genuine turning of mind and heart toward God that bears fruit in a changed life.
The word pisteuete calls for belief, for trusting the good news.
Not merely admiring Jesus from a distance.
Not merely agreeing that He existed.
But entrusting ourselves to Him as Savior and Lord.
And maybe this is the moment where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because perhaps you have spent years trying to convince everyone that you are doing well.
You have mastered the language of faith.
You know the songs.
You know the Scriptures.
You know when to raise your hands during worship.
But there is a room in your heart that you have kept locked.
A place where shame has been living.
A place where old wounds still bleed.
A place where sin has been quietly negotiating with your conscience.
And you are afraid that if the door opens, everything will fall apart.
But listen carefully.
Jesus did not come because humanity had successfully concealed its sin.
He came because humanity needed saving.
He already knows the truth.
The failure you are embarrassed to confess.
The compromise you regret.
The prayer you are afraid to pray.
The nights you wondered whether God could still receive someone like you.
And His invitation is not to continue pretending.
It is to come into the light.
First John 1:9 promises:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
That promise is not permission to remain in sin.
It is hope for those who are ready to stop hiding.
You do not have to defend the very thing that is destroying you.
You do not have to keep calling your chains freedom.
You do not have to spend the rest of your life pretending that a divided heart is a surrendered heart.
You can repent.
You can come to Christ.
You can receive forgiveness through Him.
And by the power of the Holy Spirit, you can begin walking in new obedience.
Not because you have become strong enough to save yourself.
But because the Savior is mighty to save.
Maybe your marriage is hurting.
Maybe your children have seen a side of you that your church friends have never witnessed.
Maybe you have spent so much time providing for your family that you have forgotten how to be spiritually present with them.
Maybe you have built a successful life but lost the habit of prayer.
Maybe you have spent years arguing about religion while neglecting mercy, humility, and love.
Or maybe you are reading this with tears in your eyes because you know exactly what it means to have people admire the outside while the inside is falling apart.
There is still hope in Jesus Christ.
Not a cheap hope that denies consequences.
Not a sentimental promise that every broken relationship will instantly be repaired.
Not a guarantee that repentance will erase every earthly result of past decisions.
But the living hope of a Savior who forgives, restores fellowship with God, and transforms those who belong to Him.
Sometimes restoration includes difficult conversations.
Sometimes it includes confession to people we have wounded.
Sometimes it requires accountability, patience, restitution, and years of faithful rebuilding.
Grace does not make truth unnecessary.
Grace gives us the courage to face it.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this desperately needs to hear.
You are not required to continue the spiritual patterns you inherited.
Abijah followed the sins of his father.
But the next generation did not have to remain trapped in the same direction.
His son Asa became king after him.
And 1 Kings 15:11 says:
“And Asa did that which was right in the eyes of the LORD, as did David his father.” (KJV)
The contrast is striking.
Abijah was not wholly devoted.
Asa began a reign remembered for significant reforms and faithfulness, though his own later life also contained failures.
The point is not that Asa was sinless.
The point is that the failures of one generation did not make faithful obedience impossible for the next.
And that truth deserves to reach every parent, every son, every daughter, and every wounded believer reading these words.
Your family history does not have to become your spiritual destiny.
Perhaps your father never taught you how to pray.
Perhaps your mother struggled with bitterness.
Perhaps your home was filled with arguments instead of peace.
Perhaps you learned secrecy before you learned honesty.
Perhaps you inherited wounds that you are still trying to understand.
Those experiences can leave deep marks.
But through Jesus Christ, you are not condemned to repeat every destructive pattern that came before you.
You can begin telling the truth.
You can ask for forgiveness.
You can learn to love differently.
You can teach your children what repentance looks like instead of pretending that parents never make mistakes.
You can become the person who says, “This pattern ends here, by the grace of God.”
And when you fail, you can return to Christ rather than hiding behind pride.
That is what real spiritual transformation looks like.
Not perfection performed for an audience.
But a life increasingly surrendered to the Lord.
And there is one more detail in Abijah's story that should stop us in our tracks.
His fifty-two children are counted.
But most of their personal stories are not told.
We know their number.
We do not know their names from this passage.
We know their father possessed a royal household.
We do not know the private struggles each one carried.
And there is something deeply moving about that silence.
Because behind every number is a human life.
Behind every family statistic is a person who matters to God.
Behind every congregation attendance figure is someone who may be silently suffering.
Behind every follower count is a soul.
That is why Gospel ministry must never become merely a competition for numbers.
Numbers can tell us how far a message has traveled.
They cannot tell us everything God is doing in a human heart.
A million views cannot substitute for faithfulness to Scripture.
A thousand comments cannot replace repentance.
And a growing ministry is not automatically a spiritually healthy ministry.
Our calling is to proclaim Christ faithfully and entrust the results to God.
Because the goal is not simply to make people react.
It is to help people encounter the truth of God's Word and respond to Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is why this little-known verse deserves to be remembered.
Not because fourteen wives and fifty-two children make a sensational headline.
But because beneath those numbers lies a question every human being must eventually face.
What good is an impressive life if the heart remains far from God?
Dear reader, if this story has exposed something you have been avoiding, do not rush past that conviction.
Take it to Jesus.
If you need to confess sin, confess it.
If you need to ask forgiveness, begin.
If you need to return to prayer, return.
If you need to open your Bible again after months of neglect, open it.
If you need the help of a trusted pastor or mature believer, seek it.
And if you have never truly placed your faith in Christ, hear His invitation today.
You do not have to arrive with a perfect past.
You come as a sinner in need of grace.
And you come to a Savior who is sufficient.
You may pray something like this, not as a magical formula, but as a sincere expression of repentance and faith:

“Lord Jesus, You know everything about me. You know what I have hidden, what I have justified, and what I have been afraid to surrender. I confess that I have sinned against You. I cannot save myself. I believe that You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me, change my heart, and teach me to follow You. I do not want a life that only looks faithful from the outside. I want to belong to You completely. In Your name, amen.”
And if that prayer expresses the genuine desire of your heart, do not stop at an emotional moment.
Continue in the Word.
Seek fellowship with faithful believers.
Learn what Jesus taught.
Obey Him.
Grow in grace.
Because discipleship is not a single dramatic feeling.
It is a lifelong journey of following the One who saved us.
You do not have to expose private details or share anything that would put you or someone else at risk.
And if Christ has already begun restoring areas of your life that once seemed hopeless, consider sharing a short testimony.
Someone reading may be wondering whether genuine change is possible.
Your testimony could remind them that God's grace is not an empty religious slogan.
It is the power of God at work in real lives.
And please, do not let this message end with you.
Not because following a page makes anyone right with God.
But because regular exposure to Scripture, sound teaching, encouragement, and honest conversations about faith can help people continue seeking the truth.
There is a difference between enjoying a message and helping make it possible for more people to receive one.
Every carefully researched article, every biblical resource, every devotional, and every effort to reach another struggling soul requires time, work, and practical support.
For those who view financial giving as part of their Christian stewardship, supporting faithful Gospel work can be one meaningful expression of that generosity.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
That is the kind of support we desire.
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
Not a transaction for God's favor.
But willing generosity flowing from love for Christ and a desire to see His truth reach others.
Those resources are intended to help believers grow deeper in Jesus Christ, strengthen their understanding of Scripture, and develop habits of faithful Christian living.
But if you believe in this mission and have the means to help sustain it, your partnership would be deeply appreciated.
Perhaps someone who would never search for a sermon will stop to read a story about an ancient king with fifty-two children.
Perhaps they will recognize their own divided heart.
Perhaps they will open a Bible.
Perhaps they will begin asking questions about Jesus.
But we can faithfully place the truth before others and pray that He uses it for His glory.
It is about making Jesus Christ known.
And now, before you leave, return with me one last time to that palace in ancient Judah.
Fourteen wives.
Twenty-two sons.
Sixteen daughters.
A throne.
A kingdom.
A victory in battle.
A name preserved in Scripture.
So much that people could count.
So much that people could admire.
And yet the most searching statement about Abijah was not about what he possessed.
It was about his heart.
That is what should stay with us tonight.
Not merely the extraordinary size of his family.
Not merely the brevity of his reign.
Not merely the contrast between Chronicles and Kings.
But the realization that everything people can count may still fail to reveal what matters most before God.
One day, our earthly achievements will also pass.
The applause will fade.
The possessions will change hands.
The titles will no longer belong to us.
And the question will not be whether we successfully convinced everyone that we were spiritual.
The question will be whether we truly belonged to Jesus Christ.
Not whether we were saved by our achievements.
But whether we received the Savior whose grace produces a transformed life.
Abijah's story is a warning.
Jesus Christ is our hope.
And the Gospel is the good news that our failures do not have to have the final word when we turn to Him in repentance and faith.
So if this story has reached a place in your heart that you have been afraid to confront, do not ignore it.
Bring it to the Lord.
And remember this:
You can spend your entire life building a kingdom that impresses the world, only to discover that the one throne you never surrendered was the throne of your own heart.
